ideas.hypothesis: Census tracts within a half mile of MARTA rail stations with large TOD projects (e.g., Lindbergh Center) experienced greater displacement of low- and moderate-income households than comparable station areas without TOD, and the effect is smaller where equity tools such as dedicated affordable-housing funds were applied.

mechanism: TOD disrupting low-income neighborhoods and equity tools (Denver TOD fund) as mitigation

ideas.test: Difference-in-differences using 2000 Census and 2015-2019 ACS tract data for MARTA station areas: compare change in low-income household share, rent burden and out-migration (e.g., from residential history datasets) between TOD and non-TOD station tracts, with matched non-station control tracts.
ideas.disconfirming: TOD station tracts show no greater decline in low-income share or rise in rents than non-TOD station tracts.

ideas.hypothesis: Households in TOD areas with higher pedestrian-friendly design scores and reduced parking requirements spend a smaller share of income on combined housing and transportation, with the largest savings in deprived neighbourhoods.

ideas.test: Cross-sectional block-group analysis in 3-5 US metros linking a walkability index (e.g., EPA Smart Location data) and parking minimums to the H+T affordability index, stratified by area deprivation, with income and transit service controls.
ideas.disconfirming: No association, or higher walkability linked to higher combined housing+transport cost share for low-income households.

ideas.hypothesis: Excess commuting around MARTA stations declined less than around comparable Boston MBTA stations over 1990-2010 because Atlanta's lower station-area density weakens the transport-land use connection; station-area density predicts the change in excess commuting.

ideas.test: Compute station-catchment excess commuting from CTPP journey-to-work flows for 1990, 2000 and 2010 in both regions, then regress change on station-area residential and job density.
ideas.disconfirming: Station-area density is unrelated to changes in excess commuting, or Atlanta shows equal or larger declines.

ideas.hypothesis: TOD evaluation studies that use a quantitative TOD index (regional context, land use mix, transit mode) report smaller and more consistent travel-behaviour effects than single-site case studies, indicating case-study selection bias.

ideas.test: Meta-analysis of 40-60 TOD studies 2000-2019 coding design (index-based multi-site vs single case) and effect sizes on VMT or transit mode share; meta-regression of effect size on design type.
ideas.disconfirming: Effect sizes and heterogeneity do not differ by study design.

ideas.hypothesis: Metropolitan regions receiving more federal transit research and demonstration funding adopt TOD-supporting innovations (modern streetcars, automated people movers) earlier, and these projects achieve higher ridership productivity.

ideas.disconfirming: Research funding shows no relation to adoption timing or to ridership productivity.

ideas.hypothesis: Estimates of infill development response to parking management and TOD are overstated when studies do not correct for multiple testing and specification search; applying backtest-overfitting corrections from empirical finance shrinks reported effects.
